title: Trilce: Poem IV - Two Carts Creak Against the Hammers
text:
Two carts creak against the hammers

all the way to the trifurcate tear ducts,

whennever we did nothing to them.

To that other one yes, unloved,

embittered beneath a country tunnel

for the one thing, and over hard acid

spirituous tests.


I lay myself down in the tone of a third part,

but the afternoon-what are we ggoing to ddoo with it-

rings itself in my head, furiously

refusing to be dosed into mother. These are the rings.


They are the nuptial tropics already chewed.

Going away, better than everything,

breaks into Crucible.


That not having faded

for anything. Side by side with destiny, and it weeps

and weeps. The whole song

squared in three silences.


Heat. Ovary. Almost transparency.

Everything has been wept. The whole has been watched over

in full left.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Vallejo's misspellings, neologisms, and final sequence of heat, ovary, transparency, and leftness.

title: Trilce: Poem IX - I Seak to Returrn at One Blow the Blow
text:
I seak to returrn at one blow the blow.

Its two broad leaves, its valve

opening in succulent reception

from multiplicand to multiplier,

its excellent condition for pleasure,

everything conducted truth.


I seek to returrn at one blow the blow.

At its caress, I graft Bolivarian roughnesses

to thirty-two cables and their multiples;

hair by hair, sovereign muzzles

are tightened up, the two volumes of the Work,

and then I do not live absence,

                    nor even to the touch.


I fail to returrrn at one blow the blow.

We shall never saddle the bullish Vaveo

of selfishness and of that mortal rubbing

of sheet,

since this woman

                    how much she weighs of general!


And female is the soul of the absent woman.

And female is my soul.
editorial_note: The translation mirrors the source's distorted search/return spellings and keeps the sexual-mechanical pressure.

title: Trilce: Poem X - Pristine and Final Stone of Unfounded
text:
Pristine and final stone of unfounded

fortune, she has just died

with soul and all, October room and pregnant.

Of three months absent and ten of sweet.

How destiny,

mitred monodactyl, laughs.


How behind they evict assemblies

of opposites. How the numeral always appears

beneath the line of every avatar.


How whales charge doves a fee.

How these in turn leave the beak

cubed in a third wing.

How we saddle-bow ourselves, facing monotonous haunches.


It is towed ten months toward the ten,

toward another beyond.

Two remain at least still in swaddling clothes.

And the three months of absence.

And the nine of gestation.


There is not a single violence.

The patient rises,

and seated peacocks tranquil mixtures.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's pregnancy arithmetic, mitred monodactyl, and invented verbal motions.

title: Trilce: Poem LXVI - November Second Tolls
text:
November Second tolls.


These chairs are good welcomes.

The branch of foreboding

goes, comes, rises, waves sweatily,

fatigued in this room.

November Second tolls sadly.


Dead ones, how low your abolished teeth cut,

reviewing blind nerves,

without remembering the hard fiber

that round singer-workers mend

with endless hemp, with innumerable knots

beating at a crossroads.


You, dead ones, of the clear knees,

pure by force of giving yourselves,

how you saw the other heart

with your white crowns, sparse

with cordiality. Yes. You, dead ones.


November Second tolls sadly.

And the branch of foreboding

is bitten by a cart that simply

rolls down the street.
editorial_note: The translation keeps All Souls' Day as a tolling, room-bound visitation of the dead.

title: Song of Agony
text:
If you seek to move with your song,

first your tears must spring forth;

you possess no other mirror than your whole

heart in your hand, nor any other charm


except your ardor or your brokenness.

Verse is nothing more than a subtle vein

flowing from mystery; the true one

is only that which rises with tears.


Apollo is not your servant; he only stalks

your soul with his darts, never forgetting

his crowded quiver above your hand.


But if weeping springs from the wound

of your lips, then his winged arrow too

must reach the brother heart.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the ars poetica of tears, mystery, Apollo's arrow, and shared wounded song.
